title: Migration Lock: A Small DDL Change Stops Orders
businessContext: An orders table has 80 million rows. A deployment runs ALTER TABLE while a reporting transaction holds an older snapshot and a conflicting table lock. New order traffic begins queuing behind the waiting DDL.
problemStatement: Order creation p99 reaches 30 seconds immediately after a schema migration starts; database CPU remains low. Work through three timed developments, justify your actions, and write an evidence-based incident response. The simulation starts paused; advancing time can expire unanswered decisions.
constraints: Preserve committed orders and capture blocking evidence before intervention.
Do not kill all sessions or rewrite the large table during peak traffic.
Application rollback must remain compatible with the expanded schema.
All telemetry is synthetic. Actions only affect this practice simulation.
candidateTasks: Contain customer impact while preserving evidence and data integrity.
Respond to each new development and explain the selected action.
Cite telemetry supporting the root cause; distinguish observation from inference.
Define a permanent correction, regression coverage, recovery gates, and stakeholder update.

branches.partial: Some impact remains. Cancel the conflicting DDL before retrying; the same blocker would recreate the queue.

hints: Migration PID 812 waits on PID 601 according to pg_blocking_pids.
Record session age, query text, lock modes and blocker relationships; redact customer values.
Use expand-contract releases with a short lock_timeout; keep both application versions compatible with the expanded schema.
alternativeApproaches: Schedule a reviewed low-traffic window with reporting coordination for DDL requiring stronger locks.
For an index-only change, consider CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY with its own operational constraints; it does not make arbitrary ALTER TABLE operations concurrent.
commonMistakes: Assuming every ALTER TABLE rewrites the table or that metadata-only means lock-free.
Terminating every session without inspecting blockers.
Combining DDL, full-table backfill and destructive contraction in one release.
